children: India is continuing to push Chile for “something substantive” in terms of commitments on critical mineral supplies, including copper and lithium, as the two countries seek to conclude negotiations on a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) by the year-end, sources said.

Chile is the world’s largest producer of mined copper and one of the world’s leading lithium producers. Preferential access is important for India as it seeks to diversify supplies of minerals needed for electronics manufacturing, electric vehicles, renewable energy and other industrial applications.

Despite agreeing to a separate chapter on critical minerals in the CEPA, Chile is seeking to focus on cooperation to secure supply chains and exports of value-added products rather than committing to preferential access to raw materials.
India, however, wants at least some preferential treatment in accessing critical minerals, making the issue a persistent sticking point in the negotiations, sources said.
“Some of the preferences recently sought by India for securing supplies have been mostly rejected by Chile on the grounds that they were not possible under Chile’s existing laws,” a source said.
New Delhi sees critical minerals as an important balancing factor in the proposed pact, particularly as it is opening up its large domestic market to Chile.

“We have given them our strong ask. We are giving the Chileans access to such a big market. In return we are hardly getting any market. So at least they must give us something substantive in critical minerals,” the source said.

The critical-minerals discussions also come amid growing commercial interest between the two countries. In November 2025, Chilean state-owned miner Codelco and Kutch Copper, a subsidiary of Adani Enterprises, signed an agreement to explore three copper projects in Chile, including possible joint development.

Chile is India’s fifth-largest trading partner in the Latin American and Caribbean region. In 2025, India’s exports to Chile were valued at $1.41 billion, up from $1.24 billion the previous year, while imports from Chile rose sharply to $3.97 billion from $2.59 billion, mainly due to higher gold imports, according to government figures.
Striking trade deals with Latin American countries is an important part of India’s trade diversification strategy, with the urgency rising as US tariffs hit exports.

India and Chile signed a preferential trade agreement (PTA) in 2006, which was expanded in 2017. India offered concessions on 1,031 tariff lines to Chile, while Chile offered concessions on 1,798 Indian tariff lines. The CEPA under negotiation is expected to broaden the scope of the existing agreement to cover goods, critical minerals, services, digital services, MSMEs and investment.

India’s exports to Chile comprise automobiles, pharmaceuticals, electrical machinery and equipment, textiles, chemicals, agricultural and food products, and iron and steel products. Chile’s exports to India comprise mainly bulk minerals and ores, including copper concentrate, molybdenum, iodine and gold, as well as inorganic chemicals and agricultural products such as fruits.

title: India, Chile struggle to clear critical-mineral hurdle in CEPA talks
